Causal learning & simulation across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Preschoolers are often called "little scientists," and indeed between four and five years of age, children’s causal reasoning becomes more sophisticated and rule-governed. A 4-year-old can understand simple cause-and-effect relationships and frequently asks explanatory "Why?" questions; by age 5, these abilities expand into a more systematic intuitive grasp of how the physical and social world operates (albeit with some naïve misconceptions that will be corrected in later childhood). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

By five, children parse causal structure more reliably than at four: they more consistently distinguish causation from correlation, notice when evidence is confounded, and actively intervene to resolve it during play 1. They can integrate probabilistic evidence with the results of their own actions to estimate causal strength, rather than relying on raw co-occurrence 2. They choose targeted "what if I change this?" actions (the "conditional intervention" principle; manipulating objects to isolate variables) to test a system and tell whether events form a chain, share a single cause, or require two causes together, an ability that’s noticeably less consistent at four 3; in general, children this age now have a measurable degree of metacognitive awareness of confounded evidence 4, 5 and can disambiguate the causal structure of simple systems, reflecting the emergence of scientific reasoning (in a largely implicit and context-specific manner). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Classic theory held that counterfactual reasoning didn’t emerge until age 6 or later. But newer findings suggest the beginnings appear during the 4- to 5-year window under the right conditions. In one study using an over-determined outcome (two blocks made a box light up), children were asked to mentally remove one block and predict the effect: four-year-olds answered correctly significantly more often than not, and five-year-olds were nearly perfect, while three-year-olds struggled to do better than guessing 6. This shows that by 4 or 5, kids can simulate a simple "what if" scenario in their minds, holding one factor constant and mentally undoing another to see the hypothetical result. That said, their counterfactual thinking is still fragile and very task-dependent. They often appear to skip the actual "counterfactual simulation" step 7, 8 or to maintain/alter variables inaccurately (often systematically 8); if the narrative is even slightly more complicated than the most basic presentations or the question phrased subtly, younger children often err by either overwriting reality with fantasy or failing to keep track of what changed versus what stayed the same 9, 7. For example, one study used multi-step food chains to probe 5- and 7-year-olds’ capacity for counterfactual simulation, finding that 5-year-olds typically perform at chance while 7-year-olds are accurate 10. Another study used a basic doubly-determined physical outcome to probe counterfactual reasoning, finding that 4- and 5-year-olds performed at chance levels 11. Overall, children this age can imagine a basic "what if" outcome, but, even in basic scenarios, they do not always choose the most relevant or correct one or may not even initiate a simulation in the first place. Nonetheless, the capacity to entertain alternative causal worlds (even nascently) is a huge step; it underpins their understanding of why something happened (by thinking of what would happen otherwise) and even moral/emotional concepts like guilt or relief ("If I hadn’t broken the vase, Mom wouldn’t be upset.").

Along with basic scientific reasoning and counterfactual simulation, four- to five-year-olds link hidden internal parts to causal powers, prefer common-mechanism matches over superficial similarity for generalization, and allow causal properties to "transfer" with the mechanism (e.g., moving an inner component) 12. Similarly, 4- to 5-year-olds see advancements in producing and understanding explanations of causal structures; they not only prefer satisfying explanations but also remember them better than weak ones, showing a clearer memory advantage for "good" explanations across naturalistic tasks (e.g they find "The paddle moves the boat because it pushes water backwards" more satisfying than "It moves because it moves") 13. When prompted to explain, older preschoolers increasingly privilege causally rich, inductive features over surface similarity and even boost memory for hidden (internal) properties (a tendency that strengthens as children are prompted to explain their actions/beliefs) 14. They also become more willing to revise earlier explanations in light of discrepant evidence, a flexibility that strengthens from 4 to 5 years and helps them integrate cross-domain information 15. In step with these cognitive gains, their causal language sharpens: 4-5-year-olds succeed more often at matching "because/so" to event structure and, in constrained production tasks, show markedly fewer cause-effect inversions than younger preschoolers, signaling more adult-like deployment of "because" and "so" in explanations 16. Around this age, there is also evidence that children weigh others’ explanations based on their verifiability (whether the child can verify the explanation) 17, 18, further signaling epistemic vigilance.

In summary, between ages four and five, children’s understanding of causality and physical logic becomes more principled. A 5-year-old is less fooled by mere coincidence and more interested in underlying reasons than a 4-year-old. They experiment actively and learn from interventions, embodying the scientific method in their play. Their intuitive theories about how things work (from machines to natural phenomena) are still simplistic, yet increasingly they incorporate concepts of unseen causes (germs make you sick, wires carry power, etc.).
